result:
The town had a library for things people had almost said.

It stood between a bakery and a locksmith, which seemed appropriate. Inside were narrow drawers labeled *Apologies*, *Declarations*, *Questions Asked Too Late*, and, taking up most of the eastern wall, *Things That Would Have Been Funny Ten Minutes Ago*.

You could borrow any sentence for two weeks.

A man who had never spoken at his neighborhood meetings checked out “I don’t think that’s fair.” He practiced it in the car. When he finally used it, his voice shook, but the minutes recorded his objection just as plainly as everyone else’s.

A woman borrowed “Would you like to have dinner sometime?” and returned it the next morning.

“How did it go?” the librarian asked.

“We’re going Thursday.”

The librarian stamped the card.

There were rules. You couldn’t borrow words to speak on someone else’s behalf. You couldn’t keep a sentence merely because you liked the sound of yourself saying it. Renewals were permitted, though the librarian might ask what you were waiting for.

One evening, a child arrived with an empty jam jar.

“I want to donate something.”

“What have you got?”

The child unscrewed the lid and whispered into it.

The librarian bent close enough to hear, then found a card and wrote: *I wish you’d knock before coming into my room.*

“Is it good enough?” the child asked.

“Oh, yes. We get requests for this.”

She placed the jar on the returns cart.

“Would you like to borrow it first?”
